notes.meaning: Nathan respectfully asks the king whether this takeover happened with his approval. As the Lord's prophet, Nathan had delivered God's promise about Solomon, so it seemed strange that David would change the royal succession without telling his faithful advisers.

David asks his attendants to bring Bathsheba back into the room. She had stepped outside when Nathan arrived so the king and his counselor could speak privately. Now David is ready to give her his official answer.

David makes a solemn oath in the name of the living God, praising the Lord who had rescued him from every danger in life. He promises Bathsheba that he will keep his sacred word and place Solomon on the throne before the day is over.

Bathsheba bows low to the ground to show deep respect and gratitude to David. Wishing that the king live forever proved she was not eager for his death, but only wanted God's promise to her son fulfilled.

David summons Zadok the priest, Nathan the prophet, and Benaiah the commander of the royal guard. Bringing these three key leaders together united the priests, the prophets, and the military behind Solomon.

David commands his royal guard to place Solomon on the king's personal mule and lead him down to the Gihon spring. In those days, no ordinary subject was permitted to ride the king's mount, so this act publicly announced that David had chosen Solomon as ruler.

David orders the priest and the prophet to anoint Solomon, pouring oil on him to show that God had appointed him to rule. They were to blow the ram's horn and make a loud public proclamation that Solomon was king.

David tells them to bring Solomon up to sit on the royal throne in the palace. Solomon would reign alongside David right away, ensuring an orderly handover of power over all the tribes of Israel and Judah.

Benaiah says 'Amen,' agreeing with David's plan and praying that the Lord will confirm the appointment. He asks God to be with Solomon just as He was with David, and to make Solomon's rule even greater and more prosperous than his father's.
Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah lead the royal bodyguards to carry out the king's orders immediately. They place Solomon on David's mule and escort him down to the Gihon spring.

Zadok takes the sacred horn of oil from the tent of the Lord and anoints Solomon as king. The ram's horn is blown, and the gathered crowd shouts with great excitement, declaring their loyalty to King Solomon.
The people march behind Solomon, playing flutes and celebrating with immense joy. Their shouts and music made such a thunderous roar that it felt like the ground was shaking beneath them.
Adonijah and his guests hear the noise just as their banquet is coming to an end. Joab the general catches the blast of the horn and asks why the whole city has burst into an uproar.
Jonathan, the son of Abiathar the priest, arrives while Joab is still speaking. Adonijah invites him in, assuming that such an honorable man must be carrying good news about their cause.
Jonathan quickly corrects Adonijah with bad news. He announces that King David has officially placed Solomon on the throne, ending Adonijah's bid for power.

Jonathan describes how David sent his top leaders and the royal bodyguard to escort Solomon on the king's mule. Zadok and Nathan have already anointed him at Gihon, and the roar of the city celebrating is the sound reaching Adonijah's party.
Jonathan adds that Solomon has already taken his place on the royal throne in Jerusalem. This showed everyone that Solomon was actively ruling the kingdom with David's full blessing.

David's royal servants congratulated the old king and prayed that Solomon's reign would become even greater than his own. Weak in bed, David bowed in worship and praised the God of Israel for allowing him to live to see his chosen heir take the throne.
Terror sweeps through Adonijah's gathering as soon as Jonathan finishes speaking. Realizing their plot has failed and their lives are on the line, every guest flees in panic.

Adonijah fears that the new king will execute him for treason, so he runs to the sacred altar and grabs its four corner horns. Taking hold of the altar was an appeal for mercy, asking God to protect him from sudden violence.
Solomon's court is informed that Adonijah is clinging to the altar in fear. Adonijah pleads for his life, refusing to leave until Solomon makes an oath not to execute him with the sword.

Solomon offers his brother mercy on one condition: he must prove to be a worthy and peaceful subject. If Adonijah lives faithfully, not a hair on his head will be harmed, but any future rebellion will bring the death penalty.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern translations read this condition in strictly political terms, stating that Adonijah will live if he proves to be a loyal subject, but will die if he is found to be a traitor.

notes.meaning: Solomon has Adonijah brought down from the altar, and Adonijah bows before him, submitting to his authority as king. Solomon spares his life and orders him to go home to live quietly in private life.
